title: Can four L shaped tiles cover this twelve square region?
description: A region of twelve squares is covered by L shaped tiles of three squares each. Four tiles are needed, and they are placed one corner at a time, starting at the top left. A last count checks that every square is covered once.
teaching_notes: One idea: start at a corner square and place the tile that must cover it, then continue. Watch for students who forget the L tile may be turned.

video_script.why: The child covers a region with L shaped tiles by placing them one at a time, turning each as needed.
video_script.substitution: Twelve squares divided by three squares for each tile needs four tiles.
video_script.anchor: A region of 12 unit squares, with two rows of 2 squares at the top left and two rows of 4 squares below, and an L tile of 3 unit squares.
video_script.payoff_line: Yes, it is possible, with four L tiles turned to different positions.

final_answer.value: Yes, it is possible: four L tiles, turned to different positions
final_answer.spoken: yes, it is possible, with four L tiles turned to different positions

hold_back: Yes, it is possible: four L tiles, turned to different positions
maths_rules: 12 squares, and each L tile covers 3, so 12 ÷ 3 = 4 tiles are needed.
An L covers row 1 column 1, row 1 column 2 and row 2 column 1.
Row 2 column 2 goes with row 3 columns 2 and 3 in an L.
Row 3 column 1 goes with row 4 columns 1 and 2 in an L.
Row 3 column 4 goes with row 4 columns 3 and 4 in an L.
Check: 4 tiles of 3 squares cover 12 squares, with no gaps and no overlaps.
video_script.design: One region and one L tile. The tiles are placed in turn, starting from the top left square, each turned to fit. The method is the same as the examples in the book: place a tile, then fill what is left.
